The cornett (also called the wooden horn, H-S 423.21) is an aerophone of the European historical culture area, current between 1500 and 1650. It sounds by vibrating the lips against a cup mouthpiece, its body is mostly of curved wood, and it has six fingerholes and a thumbhole, sharing features of both the trumpet and the woodwind. The player controls pitch with the holes, cross-fingerings and embouchure. Professional players used it for state and ceremonial music, especially to accompany choirs, and it also appeared in popular music such as loud wind ensembles.

辛克號／木號屬氣鳴樂器，見於中世紀、文藝復興與巴洛克時期，約1500至1650年: The cornett is an aerophone of the Middle Ages, the Renaissance and the Baroque, in use roughly from 1500 to 1650, that is, from the end of the fifteenth century to the end of the seventeenth. Its predecessor may be connected with perforated cattle- and sheep-horn instruments, which are still played in Scandinavia, such as the Norwegian bukkehorn and the Swedish bockhorn, and the Russian shepherd's pipe is similar. Professional players used it for state and ceremonial music, especially to accompany choirs, and it also appeared in loud wind line-ups such as treble wind ensembles; in Germany it was popular because trumpet playing was restricted to the professional trumpeters' guild. After the seventeenth century the bass type was replaced by the serpent; around 1836 the old name passed to the modern cornet, and this instrument took the spelling cornett.
辛克號／木號管身多以胡桃木、黃楊木或李、櫻桃、梨等木材製成，外覆薄黑皮革或羊皮紙: The body of the cornett is mostly made of walnut, boxwood, or the wood of plum, cherry or pear, covered with thin black leather or parchment; a few are turned from a single piece of wood and bent with steam. The mouthpiece is mostly of horn, ivory or bone, and the thin tube is wound with thread for tuning; the mouthpiece socket is sometimes reinforced with a brass ring, and German and Austrian instruments may have silver or brass ferrules at both ends. The mute cornett is mostly of boxwood, with the mouthpiece and body in one piece. The straight cornett is often of uncovered boxwood. The source does not state the materials of the other parts.
